The binary symmetric channel with crossover probability p has channel matrix
(1−pp​p1−p​).​

Maximum-likelihood decoding chooses a codeword c maximizing P(Y=y∣X=c), while minimum-distance decoding chooses one minimizing the Hamming distance dH​(c,y). For a block of length n sent through a binary symmetric channel,
P(Y=y∣X=c)=pdH​(c,y)(1−p)n−dH​(c,y)=(1−p)n(1−pp​)dH​(c,y).
(15)
When p<1/2, the final factor decreases strictly with the distance. Thus maximum-likelihood and minimum-distance decoding agree.

Let RSS0​ and RSS1​ be the residual sums of squares under the restricted model with p0​ coefficients and the full model with p coefficients. Assuming X has full column rank, the nested-model F-test uses
F=RSS1​/(n−p)(RSS0​−RSS1​)/(p−p0​)​.​
(24)
Under the null hypothesis this has the Fp−p0​,n−p​ distribution.
Maximizing the Gaussian likelihood over β and the unknown variance gives σ2=RSS/n. Thus the likelihood-ratio test statistic is
−2logΛ=nlogRSS1​RSS0​​.
(25)
Since
RSS1​RSS0​​=1+n−pp−p0​​F,
(26)
we obtain
−2logΛ=nlog(1+n−pp−p0​​F).​
(27)
The logarithm is strictly increasing, so the two test statistics give exactly the same rejection ordering.

The no-cloning theorem for two pure states states that no single unitary operator can clone two distinct nonorthogonal states. Suppose, to the contrary, that
U∣αj​⟩∣0⟩=∣αj​⟩∣αj​⟩,j=0,1.
(58)
Preservation of the inner product by U gives
⟨α0​∣α1​⟩=⟨α0​∣α1​⟩2.
(59)
Writing z=⟨α0​∣α1​⟩, this requires z=0 or z=1. The first case is orthogonality; the second means that the normalized states represent the same ray. Both contradict the assumptions. Therefore distinct nonorthogonal quantum states cannot be cloned by a unitary process.

For f∈C[0,1], define its Bernstein polynomial
Bn​f(x)=∑k=0n​f(nk​)(kn​)xk(1−x)n−k.
(60)
If Xn,x​∼Bin(n,x), then
Bn​f(x)=Ef(Xn,x​/n),E(Xn,x​/n)=x,Var(Xn,x​/n)=nx(1−x)​≤4n1​.
(61)
Let M=∥f∥∞​. By uniform continuity, for any ε>0 choose δ>0 such that ∣f(u)−f(v)∣<ε/2 whenever ∣u−v∣<δ. Splitting the expectation according to that event and using Chebyshev's inequality gives, uniformly in x,
∣Bn​f(x)−f(x)∣≤2ε​+2MP(∣Xn,x​/n−x∣≥δ)≤2ε​+2nδ2M​.
(62)
For sufficiently large n this is below ε. Thus Bn​f→f uniformly on [0,1]. An affine change of variable treats every compact interval, proving the Weierstrass approximation theorem.

False. Take the bounded nonconstant continuous function f(x)=sinx. If polynomials Pn​ converged uniformly to f on R, then each sufficiently late Pn​ would be bounded on R and hence constant. A uniform limit of constants is constant, a contradiction. More generally, the globally uniform limit of real polynomials is itself a polynomial.

False. The bounded continuous function f(x)=sin(1/x) on (0,1] has no limit at zero. If polynomials converged uniformly to it there, they would be uniformly Cauchy on (0,1] and hence on [0,1] by continuity at zero. Their uniform limit on [0,1] would continuously extend f to zero, which is impossible.

12H OurBigBook.com
In the RSA cryptosystem, choose distinct primes p,q, set N=pq, and choose e with gcd(e,ϕ(N))=1. The public key is (N,e); the private exponent satisfies
ed≡1(modϕ(N)).
(68)
A message m is encrypted and decrypted by
c≡me(modN),m≡cd(modN).
(69)
Suppose ϕ(N)∣2ab, where b is odd. For a unit x modulo N, both Op​(xb) and Oq​(xb) are powers of two dividing 2a. If these orders differ, assume without loss of generality that
Op​(xb)=2r<2s=Oq​(xb).
(70)
Taking t=r<a gives
x2tb≡1(modp),x2tb≡1(modq),
(71)
and hence
gcd(x2tb−1,N)=p,​
(72)
a nontrivial factor.
To count successful x, write p−1=2ru and q−1=2sv with u,v odd. Raising to the odd power b, which is divisible by the odd parts, maps a uniformly chosen element of each cyclic multiplicative group uniformly onto its Sylow two-subgroup. In a cyclic group of order 2r, the probability of order 1 is 2−r and that of order 2j is 2j−1−r for 1≤j≤r. If r≤s, the probability that the two resulting orders agree is
2r+s1+∑j=1r​4j−1​=3⋅2r+s4r+2​≤21​.
(73)
Thus at least half of the ϕ(N) units satisfy Op​(xb)=Oq​(xb).
Knowing d reveals the multiple ed−1 of ϕ(N). Writing ed−1=2ab with b odd and trying random units therefore yields a factor with probability at least one half per trial; nonunits already reveal a factor by taking their greatest common divisor with N. Conversely, factoring N gives ϕ(N) and hence d=e−1(modϕ(N)). This proves that recovering the private key is computationally equivalent, up to randomized polynomial-time work, to factoring the RSA modulus, as summarized by RSA private exponent reveals the factorization.
For N=77 and e=43, ϕ(N)=60 and
d≡43−1≡7(mod60).
(74)
Therefore
m≡57≡47(mod77).​
(75)
Finally, e is odd because it is coprime to the even integer ϕ(N). If me≡m(modN), then
(N−m)e≡(−m)e≡−me≡−m≡N−m(modN).
(76)
Thus fixed points occur in complementary pairs m,N−m, which is the Complementary RSA fixed points property.

A branch point of a multivalued analytic function is a point around which analytic continuation along a closed loop can return a different value. A branch cut is a curve or union of curves removed from the domain so that loops causing this monodromy are excluded and one single-valued branch can be chosen.

The Knaster–Tarski fixed-point theorem states that if L is a complete lattice and f:L→L is order-preserving, then the fixed points of f form a complete lattice; in particular, f has least and greatest fixed points.
Let
P={x∈L:f(x)≤x},a=⋀P.
(100)
For every x∈P, monotonicity gives f(a)≤f(x)≤x, so f(a)≤a. Applying f once more shows f(f(a))≤f(a), hence f(a)∈P. Therefore a≤f(a) by the definition of a, and f(a)=a. Every fixed point belongs to P, so a is the least fixed point. Dually, ⋁{x:x≤f(x)} is the greatest fixed point. For any family S of fixed points, apply the same argument inside the upper interval above ⋁S to obtain the least fixed point above every member of S; this is their join in the fixed-point set. The dual construction supplies meets, proving the full statement.
To deduce the Cantor-Schröder-Bernstein theorem, let i:A→B and j:B→A be injections. On the complete lattice P(A) define
F(X)=A∖j(B∖i(X)).
(101)
This map is order-preserving, so it has a fixed point X. The relation
A∖X=j(B∖i(X))
(102)
shows that
h(a)={i(a),j−1(a),​a∈X,a∈/X​
(103)
is a bijection: its two pieces map bijectively onto the disjoint sets i(X) and B∖i(X). Thus injections both ways imply a bijection.
Let P be the poset of countable subsets of R. The family of all singletons {{r}:r∈R} has no upper bound in P, since any upper bound would contain every real number and would be uncountable. Therefore
P is not complete.​
(104)
Finally, use the well-ordering theorem to fix a well-order ≺ of R. Every countable A omits some real number; let m(A) be its ≺-least omitted element and define
f(A)=A∪{m(A)}.
(105)
If A⊆B, then either m(A)∈B, or every point preceding m(A) lies in A⊆B and m(A)=m(B). In either case f(A)⊆f(B), so f is order-preserving. Yet m(A)∈/A, and hence
f(A)=A for every A∈P.​
(106)
This does not contradict Knaster–Tarski because P is not a complete lattice.

We first prove the required case of Menger's theorem directly. Split each vertex v into vmin​ and vmout​ joined by a directed edge of capacity one. Replace every graph edge uv by the two directed edges umout​vmin​ and vmout​umin​ of capacity k, add a source joined to every ain​ for a∈A, and join every bout​ for b∈B to a sink, using unit capacities at the ends.
Starting with zero integral flow, repeatedly augment by one along a source-to-sink path in the residual directed graph. If fewer than k augmentations have occurred and no augmenting path remains, let R be the residual-reachable vertices. The capacity from R to its complement equals the current flow: every forward edge in this cut is saturated and every reverse edge carries zero flow, by residual reachability. Since the cut has capacity below k, it uses no capacity-k graph edge. The original vertices whose unit-capacity split or endpoint edges cross the cut form an AB-separator of size below k, contrary to the hypothesis. Hence at least k augmentations occur. The resulting integral flow decomposes into k source-to-sink paths, and the unit split capacities make their corresponding AB paths vertex-disjoint. This proves
there are k vertex-disjoint AB-paths.​
(107)
The same augmenting-path proof, with the source vertex given capacity k, yields the fan lemma: from a vertex x to any set of at least k vertices in a k-connected graph, there is a k-fan with distinct endpoints.
Now let C be a longest cycle in a finite k-connected graph G. If C is not Hamiltonian, choose x∈/C. A k-fan from x to C has k distinct attachment vertices. If ∣C∣<2k, two consecutive attachment vertices on C are joined by an edge of C, because the k cyclic gaps cannot all have length at least two. The two corresponding fan paths form, through x, an alternative path of length at least two between those adjacent vertices. Replacing their edge on C by this path creates a longer cycle, a contradiction. Therefore
∣C∣≥min{∣G∣,2k}.​
(108)
This is the Dirac circumference theorem; in particular, a k-connected graph contains a cycle of length at least k, and when ∣G∣≥2k it must contain one of length at least 2k.
For k=3, every 3-connected graph with at least six vertices consequently has a cycle of length at least six. This cannot be improved: the complete bipartite graph K3,m​ is 3-connected for m≥3, but every cycle alternates between its two parts and therefore has length at most six. Taking m arbitrarily large defeats every proposed bound above six. Hence
n=6.​
(109)

The splitting field of f∈K[t] is the smallest extension L/K in which f is a product of linear factors; equivalently, L is generated over K by all its roots of a polynomial. To prove existence and uniqueness of splitting fields, adjoin a root of an irreducible polynomial dividing f and repeat until f splits. If L and L′ are two resulting fields, an embedding between the fields generated so far extends by sending each newly adjoined root to a root of its transformed minimal polynomial. Repetition gives a K-embedding L→L′, whose image contains every root of f and is therefore all of L′. Thus the splitting field exists and is unique up to K-isomorphism.
Now write K=Fq​, and let the distinct irreducible factors of f have degrees d1​,…,dr​. The irreducible factors of a finite-field Frobenius polynomial show that a root of the degree-di​ factor lies in Fqn​ exactly when di​∣n. Hence the splitting field over a finite field is
L=Fqm​,[L:K]=m=lcm(d1​,…,dr​)​.
(110)
Every finite field is a perfect field, so L/K is separable; it is normal because it is a splitting field. It is consequently a Galois extension. More explicitly, the Galois group of a finite field extension is the cyclic group of order m generated by the finite-field Frobenius automorphism x↦xq.
Finally, let N2​(n) denote the number of monic irreducible polynomials over a finite field of degree n over F2​. Since
Nq​(n)=n1​∑d∣n​μ(d)qn/d,

The Simplicial approximation theorem states that if K is a finite simplicial complex, L is a simplicial complex, and f:∣K∣→∣L∣ is continuous, then for some r≥0 there is a simplicial approximation g:K(r)→L to f.
The target open stars form an open cover of ∣L∣, so their inverse images under f form an open cover of the compact metric space ∣K∣. The Lebesgue number lemma supplies δ>0 such that every subset of diameter below δ lies in one inverse image. Choose r so large that every vertex star in K(r) has diameter below δ; this is possible because its diameter is at most twice μ(K(r)) and the mesh tends to zero.
For each vertex v choose a vertex w(v) of L such that
f(stK(r)​(v))⊆stL​(w(v)).
(140)
If v0​,…,vq​ span a simplex, a point in its relative interior belongs to all their open stars. Its image belongs to all the open stars of w(v0​),…,w(vq​), so these target vertices span a simplex. Thus v↦w(v) extends to a simplicial map g, and its defining inclusion says exactly that g approximates f. This proves the theorem.

A bounded linear operator T:X→Y is a compact operator when the image of the closed unit ball has compact closure, equivalently when every bounded sequence (xn​) has a subsequence for which (Txn​) converges.
Each Ti​ is compact because its image lies in a finite-dimensional subspace. Let BX​ be the unit ball and fix ε>0. Choose i with ∥T−Ti​∥<ε/3. Since Ti​(BX​) is relatively compact, it has a finite ε/3-net y1​,…,yN​. For each x∈BX​, choose yj​ with ∥Ti​x−yj​∥<ε/3; then
∥Tx−yj​∥≤∥(T−Ti​)x∥+∥Ti​x−yj​∥<32ε​.
(142)
Thus T(BX​) is totally bounded. Its closure is complete because Y is a Banach space, so it is compact. This proves the norm-closedness of compact operators and hence
T is compact.​

The uniformization theorem states that every simply connected Riemann surface is biholomorphic to exactly one of the Riemann sphere C, the complex plane C, or the unit disc D. A surface is uniformized by one of these when that surface is its universal cover. The only surface uniformized by C is the sphere itself, because every nonidentity Möbius transformation has a fixed point and therefore cannot act as a deck transformation. The Riemann surfaces uniformized by the complex plane are
C,C∗,C/Λ for a lattice Λ.​
(149)
Let U⊆C have a complement containing at least two points. Its universal cover cannot be the sphere because U is noncompact. If it were the plane, the covering map C→U↪C would be a nonconstant entire function omitting two values, contrary to the Little Picard theorem. The plane domain with two omitted points is hyperbolic, so

The pionic-deuterium ground state has atomic ℓ=0. Since the pion has spin zero, its total angular momentum is therefore the deuteron spin, J=1, and its parity is ηd​ηπ​=ηπ​. The two neutrons are identical fermions. Their antisymmetric spin-one-half singlet state would require even orbital ℓ, but S=0 and J=1 would instead require ℓ=1. Hence they must occupy the symmetric spin-one-half triplet state, so the orbital state is antisymmetric and ℓ is odd. The addition of angular momentum with S=J=1 permits ℓ=0,1,2, leaving ℓ=1. Thus parity conservation gives
ηπ​=ηn2​(−1)1=−1,
(252)
so the pion has intrinsic parity ηπ​=−1​.
In Δ−→π−+n, the final total spin is S=1/2. Coupling it to ℓ to obtain J=3/2 gives
​ℓ−21​​≤23​≤ℓ+21​,
(253)
so the allowed orbital angular momenta are ℓ=1,2​. The observed angular probability is cos2θ=∣P1​(cosθ)∣2, where P1​ is a Legendre polynomial; it therefore selects the ℓ=1 partial wave rather than ℓ=2. The parity selection rule for a two-body decay now gives
ηΔ−​=ηπ​ηn​(−1)ℓ=(−1)(+1)(−1)=+1.
(254)
Therefore the delta particle has intrinsic parity ηΔ−​=+1​.

Label the two atoms in primitive cell j by u2j​ and u2j+1​, with j understood modulo N because of the periodic boundary condition. Choose the spring between them to have constant λ. Newton's second law gives
mu¨2j​mu¨2j+1​​=λ(u2j+1​−u2j​)+αλ(u2j−1​−u2j​),=λ(u2j​−u2j+1​)+αλ(u2j+2​−u2j+1​).​
(255)
For a longitudinal normal mode, put
u2j​=Aei(2jka−ωt),u2j+1​=Bei((2j+1)ka−ωt).
(256)
Periodicity requires e2iNka=1, so k=πr/(Na). Since the primitive-cell length is 2a, wavevectors differing by π/a describe the same mode, and the first Brillouin zone may be chosen as
−2aπ​≤k<2aπ​.​
(257)
The amplitudes obey
(λ(1+α)−mω2−λ(e−ika+αeika)​−λ(eika+αe−ika)λ(1+α)−mω2​)(AB​)=0.
(258)
Setting its determinant to zero gives the alternating-spring chain dispersion relation
ω±2​(k)=mλ​[1+α±(1−α)2+4αcos2(ka)​].​
(259)
The lower sign is the acoustic phonon branch and the upper sign is the optical phonon branch.
At the edge of the Brillouin zone,
ω±2​=mλ​(1+α±∣1−α∣),
(260)
so the frequency band gap is
Δω=m2λ​​∣1−α​∣.​
(261)
It vanishes at α=1, when the apparent two-atom primitive cell can be reduced to one atom.
Near the centre of the Brillouin zone, a Taylor expansion gives
ω−​(k)=am(1+α)2αλ​​∣k∣+O(∣k∣3),​
(262)
and
ω+​(k)=m2λ(1+α)​​[1−2(1+α)2αa2k2​+O(k4)].​
(263)
The group velocity of the acoustic branch at long wavelength is the speed of sound,
cs​=am(1+α)2αλ​​.​
(264)

f(v)=(2πkB​Tm​)3/2exp(−2kB​Tm∣v∣2​).​

g(v)=4πv2(2πkB​Tm​)3/2e−mv2/(2kB​T),v≥0.​

dvd​logg(v)=v2​−kB​Tmv​,

b OurBigBook.com
For pressureless matter, w=0 and part (a) gives ρ=3μ/(8πa3). With Λ=0, the Friedmann equation becomes
a˙2+k=aμ​,
(279)
or
a˙2+V(a)=C,V(a)=−aμ​,C=−k.​
(280)
This is the Λ=0 case of the Friedmann effective potential for pressureless matter. The potential rises monotonically from −∞ at a=0 to zero from below as a→∞.
For k=+1, C=−1 intersects the potential at amax​=μ. An initially expanding closed matter-dominated Friedmann solution reaches this turning point and recollapses to a Big Crunch. For k=0, C=0 gives expansion for all time with a˙→0 and a∝t2/3. For k=−1, C=1 gives eternal expansion with a˙→1 in these units. Thus positive curvature recollapses, whereas zero and negative curvature expand forever.

For Λ>0 and k=1,
V(a)=−aμ​−3Λa2​,C=−1.
(285)
The unique maximum occurs at
aE​=(2Λ3μ​)1/3,Vmax​=−ΛaE2​.

The critical closed matter-cosmological-constant universe is obtained from Vmax​=−1:
Λcrit​=9μ24​,aE​=23μ​=Λcrit−1/2​.​
(287)
If Λ>Λcrit​, then Vmax​<−1: the energy line lies above the barrier, and a universe expanding from a=0 passes over it and expands forever toward de Sitter behavior. If Λ=Λcrit​, the exact solution at a=aE​ is the Einstein static universe; the Big-Bang branch approaches it only asymptotically, while a separate branch can emerge from it and expand forever. If 0<Λ<Λcrit​, the equation V(a)=−1 has two positive roots a−​<aE​<a+​. The Big-Bang branch expands to a−​ and recollapses, while the disconnected large-a branch contracts to a+​ and undergoes a Friedmann bounce for pressureless matter and positive cosmological constant. These are all qualitatively different possibilities.

Take k>0; reflection in x supplies the result for negative wavenumber. Since each region has uniform base velocity, the perturbation is an incompressible, irrotational flow with a velocity potential satisfying the Laplace equation. Its decaying outer forms are
ϕ+​=A+​e−k(y−h)eikx+σt,ϕ−​=A−​ek(y+h)eikx+σt.
(288)
For a varicose mode of a planar jet, reflection symmetry makes the inner potential proportional to cosh(ky); for a sinuous mode of a planar jet, it is proportional to sinh(ky).
At the upper interface, the linearized kinematic boundary condition is
ση=∂y​ϕ+​(h),(σ+ikU)η=∂y​ϕin​(h).
(289)
The first equation gives ϕ+​(h)=−ση/k. The second gives
ϕin​(h)=kσ+ikU​η{coth(kh),tanh(kh),​varicose,sinuous.​
(290)
The linearized Unsteady Bernoulli equation gives p′=−ρ(∂t​+U∂x​)ϕ. Applying pressure continuity therefore produces the equal-density top-hat planar-jet dispersion relation
σ2+F(σ+ikU)2=0,​F={coth(kh),tanh(kh),​varicose,sinuous.​
(291)
Solving the quadratic equation gives
σ=1+FkU​(±F​−iF).
(292)
Equivalently,
σvar​σsin​​=±2kU​1−e−4kh​−2ikU​(1+e−2kh),=±2kU​1−e−4kh​−2ikU​(1−e−2kh).​​
(293)
The plus sign is the unstable Kelvin-Helmholtz instability branch. In particular, the two modes have exactly the same growth rate,
σR​(k)=2kU​1−e−4kh​.​
(294)
Its limiting forms are
σR​∼Uh​k3/2(kh→0),σR​∼2Uk​(kh→∞).​
(295)
Thus neither type grows faster in this equal-density idealization, although their phase speeds differ. The unbounded large-k growth is the familiar short-wave pathology of an inviscid vortex sheet.

Work in the shock frame. The undisturbed upstream gas enters the stationary discontinuity at speed
w1​=U,
(296)
while the downstream gas, which moves with the piston in the laboratory frame, leaves at
w2​=U−V.
(297)
The Rankine-Hugoniot conditions for a perfect gas are
ρ1​U=ρ2​(U−V),
(298)
p1​+ρ1​U2=p2​+ρ2​(U−V)2,
(299)
and
(γ−1)ρ1​γp1​​+2U2​=(γ−1)ρ2​γp2​​+2(U−V)2​.
(300)
Eliminating the velocities between these equations gives the perfect-gas density jump
ρ1​ρ2​​=2γ+(γ−1)β2γ+(γ+1)β​,p2​=(1+β)p1​.
(301)
The mass and momentum equations also imply
p2​−p1​=ρ1​U2−ρ2​(U−V)2=ρ1​UV,
(302)
so
V=ρ1​Uβp1​​.
(303)
Substitution of the density ratio into mass conservation, followed by this momentum relation, gives
U2=ρ1​p1​​[γ+2γ+1​β].
(304)
Using the adiabatic sound speed c12​=γp1​/ρ1​ therefore yields
c12​U2​=1+2γγ+1​β.​
(305)
Finally, eliminating U from V=βp1​/(ρ1​U) gives the piston-driven normal shock relation
V2=2γ+(γ+1)β2β2​ρ1​p1​​.​
(306)
For a compressive shock β>0, the first boxed equation has U>c1​: the shock propagates supersonically into the undisturbed gas, approaching the sound speed in the weak shock limit β→0.

c OurBigBook.com
A stationary iterative method for a linear system converges from every initial vector exactly when the spectral radius of its iteration matrix is less than one. Here cos(kx) ranges between cosx and −cosx, so all modes decay for a fixed n exactly when
−1<1−ω−ωcosx≤λk​(ω)≤1−ω+ωcosx<1.
(314)
Requiring this for every grid size gives
0<ω≤1.​
(315)
Indeed, ω≤0 leaves or amplifies the lowest mode, while any ω>1 makes the highest-mode eigenvalue tend to 1−2ω<−1 as n→∞.
The slowest mode is k=1, for which the Taylor expansion is
λ1​(ω)=1−ω+ωcosn+1π​=1−2(n+1)2ωπ2​+O(n−4).
(316)
If the initial error has a nonzero v1​ component, that component is multiplied by λ1​(ω)ν. Hence for a constant c>0 independent of n,
∥e(ν)∥ cannot in general decay faster than (1−n2c​)ν.​
(317)
This is the low-frequency obstruction to grid-independent convergence.

μω​=π/2≤θ≤πmax​∣1−ω+ωcosθ∣=max{∣1−ω∣,∣1−2ω∣}.​

For 0<ω<1, this is strictly less than one independently of n, so high-frequency error decays geometrically much faster than the low-frequency factor 1−O(n−2).
To minimize μω​, balance the endpoint magnitudes:
